food.text: The Libu, an ancient Libyan people of the Maghreb, are first documented in Egyptian records under the pharaohs Ramesses II and his successor Merneptah in the 13th century BC. These ancient Libyans lived as pastoral nomads, gathering milk, meat, hides, and wool from their goats and sheep for food and clothing.

A Neolithic society built on domestication and subsistence agriculture, richly depicted in the rock paintings of Tassili n'Ajjer, continued to predominate across the Saharan and Mediterranean Maghreb until as late as 2000 BC. This long-standing way of farming and herding carried into the early Bronze Age, shaping how Berber communities in the region got their food.

Some researchers argue that the distinctive Maritime Bell Beaker pottery style, first found near the Tagus estuary in Portugal and radiocarbon dated to as early as the 28th century BCE, emerged from seaborne contact between Iberia and Morocco in the first half of the third millennium BCE. These beaker-style vessels were used for drinking.

Rock shelters in the Tassili n'Ajjer highlands remained in use until as late as 1500 BCE, still holding Neolithic-era ceramic bowls, potsherds, and grinders alongside beads and arrowheads. These sandstone shelters served as camps for transhumant pastoralist groups moving between the highlands and the sandy lowlands.

By as early as 1500 BCE, the Garamantes, herdsmen of the Fezzan region in what is now Libya, controlled the three eastern routes linking the Mediterranean coast to lands farther south. From their capital of Germa in the Wadi Ajal, they raided north to the sea and south into the Sahel. The Garamantes also took part in the trans-Saharan slave trade, using slaves in their own communities to build and maintain underground irrigation systems known as the foggara.

art.text: A Neolithic society built on farming and animal domestication spread across the Saharan and Mediterranean Maghreb, predominating there until around 2000 BC. This way of life was richly depicted in the paintings of Tassili n'Ajjer in south-eastern Algeria.

Rock art at Tassili n'Ajjer, alongside evidence from sites such as Dhar Tichitt in Mauritania, helps trace how cattle herding spread across vast areas of the Sahara as early as 3000 to 2000 BCE. This marks some of the earliest evidence for the spread of pastoralism in the region.

Tassili n'Ajjer's rock art traditions include the Horse tradition, which began around 2000 BCE. It was then that artists in the Algerian Sahara first began depicting horses within the plateau's sandstone rock forests.

Tassili n'Ajjer's rock art is classified into five distinct traditions: Archaic, Round Head, Bovidian (Pastoral), Horse, and Camel. The Camel tradition, from around 1000 BCE onward, came last, with the Horse tradition, from around 2000 BCE, close behind. Camels appear as the main means of transport across the Sahara, in step with long-distance caravan routes that carried salt, goods, and enslaved people. Camel-period scenes show men, mounted and on foot, armed with shields, spears, and swords.

The highlands of Tassili n'Ajjer show evidence of occupation by Neolithic pastoralist groups as late as 1500 BCE. Rock shelters scattered through its sandstone forests held ceramic pots and potsherds left behind by these inhabitants.

Alongside pottery, these Tassili n'Ajjer rock shelters yielded beads, jewelry, lithic arrowheads, bowls, and grinders. This range of crafted objects shows what Neolithic pastoralists made and carried into the Sahara highlands.

war.text: The Libu were an ancient Berber people of North Africa. They are first documented in Egyptian records from the Late Bronze Age, with the oldest known references coming from the reigns of pharaohs Ramesses II and Merneptah in the 13th century BC.

In 1208 BCE, the fifth year of Merneptah's reign, hostilities broke out between Egypt and Libya. A coalition of the Libu and Sea Peoples, led by the Libu chief Meryey, was defeated. Years later, Ramesses III defeated the Libyans in the 5th year of his reign, and six years after that the Libyans joined the Meshwesh, invaded the western Delta, and were defeated once again.
The Meshwesh were an ancient Libyan tribe. They first appear in Egyptian records during the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt, under Pharaoh Amenhotep III, around 1390 to 1350 BC.
The name Libu appears as an ethnic label on the Merneptah Stele, an ancient Egyptian inscription. The stele is also known as the Israel Stele.
Beginning around 1295 BC, in Egypt's 19th Dynasty, the Meshwesh entered a period of conflict with the Egyptian state. This near-constant warfare would continue for generations.

During Year 5 of Pharaoh Merneptah's reign, a breakdown in Egypt's early-warning system allowed an unexpected Libyan invasion of the Nile Delta and the oases of the Western Desert. The invasion was led chiefly by the Libu, joined by the Meshwesh and Sea Peoples.
Pharaoh Merneptah claimed his forces captured 9,100 swords from the Meshwesh. This happened during the repelled Libyan invasion of his fifth regnal year.

Merneptah claimed to have killed 6,000 enemy soldiers and taken 9,000 prisoners in defeating the Libyan-led invasion. To be sure of the numbers, he cut the penises off all the uncircumcised enemy dead and the hands off all the circumcised. From this, history learns that the Ekwesh were circumcised, a fact that leads some to doubt they were Greek.

politics.text: The Libu, a people of North Africa west of the Nile, are attested since the Late Bronze Age. Egyptian texts write the name as R'bw. The Greek word Libyē, later used for the whole region, came from Berber Libu.

The historian Oric Bates considered all the Libyan tribes to be a single civilization around 3000 BC, united under central Libu and Meshwesh control. He placed it mainly around Cyrenaica and Marsa matruh.

In Merneptah's fifth year (1208 BC), an army of 40,000 men and a confederacy of tribes, led by King Meryey of the Libu, fought a war against pharaoh Merneptah. It ended in defeat for Meryey and was recorded in the Great Karnak Inscription.

During the 19th and 20th dynasties (c. 1295 to 1075 BC), the Meshwesh, an ancient Libyan tribe, were in almost constant conflict with the Egyptian state. Their earliest records date back to the reign of Amenhotep III.

The oldest documented references to the Libu date to Ramesses II and his successor Merneptah, pharaohs of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, in the 13th century BC. On the Merneptah Stele, LBW appears as an ethnic name designating Libyans.
According to the Great Karnak Inscription, Meryey's military alliance was not only Libyan. It included the Meshwesh, the Lukka, and Sea Peoples known as the Ekwesh, Teresh, Shekelesh and Sherden.

Merneptah's victory over the Libu and their Sea Peoples allies came at a six-hour battle at the city of Perire, probably on the western edge of the Nile Delta. He claimed his army killed 6,000 soldiers and took 9,000 prisoners, after which the surviving Nine Bows threw down their weapons, abandoned their baggage and dependents, and ran for their lives. To be sure of the numbers, he says he took the penises of all the uncircumcised enemy dead and the hands of all the circumcised, which is how history learns that the Ekwesh were circumcised, a fact that makes some doubt they were Greek.

The Merneptah Stele has 28 lines, and most of its text glorifies his victory over the Libyans and their allies, who had invaded Egypt from the west. Only the last three lines turn to a separate campaign in Canaan, then part of Egypt's imperial possessions, where Merneptah says he defeated and destroyed Asqaluna, Gezer, Yanoam and Israel. The phrase "wasted, bare of seed" is a formula for defeated nations. It implies their grain stores were destroyed, which would bring famine the following year.
Ramesses III defeated the Libyans in the fifth year of his reign. Six years later the Libyans joined the Meshwesh and invaded the western Delta, and they were defeated once again.
By the early 12th century, Egypt claimed overlordship of the Cyrenaican tribes. At one point a ruler chosen by Egypt was set up, briefly, over the combined tribes of the Meshwesh, Libu and Soped.

Egyptian texts from the reign of Amenhotep III mention the Meshwesh as a source of cattle provided to the king's palace at Malkata. This suggests there may have been some trade relations between the Meshwesh and the Egyptians at the time.

Merneptah's confederacy enemy, called the Nine Bows, had caused such severe depredations that the western delta region was described as "forsaken as pasturage for cattle". It had been left waste from the time of the ancestors, and Merneptah fought them at Perire. After six hours the surviving Nine Bows threw down their weapons, abandoned their baggage and dependants, and ran for their lives. Merneptah states that he killed 6,000 soldiers and took 9,000 prisoners, and that to be sure of the numbers he took the penises of all uncircumcised enemy dead and the hands of all the circumcised.

Some ancient sources, such as Philistos of Syracuse, gave an "early" foundation date of around 1215 BC for Carthage, the Phoenician colony from Tyre. Modern historians generally accept the later date of 814 BC given by Timaeus.
From the reign of Akhenaten comes a remarkable papyrus showing a group of Libyans slaying an Egyptian. The papyrus is fragmentary, so its historical context is unknown.

Battle reliefs at Karnak from the reign of Seti I show the king in combat with Libyan masses. The accompanying text calls them Tjehenu, a generic Egyptian term for "Libyan", rather than naming a specific tribe.

culture.text: The Bell Beaker culture takes its name from an inverted-bell drinking vessel and first arose as early as 2800 BCE. It spread widely across western Europe and reached some coastal areas of north-western Africa, alongside Iberia, Sardinia and Sicily.

Rock art at Tassili n'Ajjer, a mountain range in south-eastern Algeria, shows that cattle were herded across vast areas as early as 3000 to 2000 BCE. This reflects one of the earliest spreads of pastoralism in the region.

From about 2000 BC, Berber languages began spreading westward from the Nile Valley, moving across the northern Sahara into the Maghreb. This spread carried the ancestors of today's Berber, or Amazigh, peoples into the region.

In the highlands of Tassili n'Ajjer, people continued living in rock shelters until as late as 1500 BCE. They left behind ceramic pots, potsherds, lithic arrowheads, bowls, grinders, beads and jewelry among the sandstone rock shelters.

The Mechta-Afalou people, also known as Paleo-Berbers, take their name from the Afalou bou Rhummel site in Béjaïa, Algeria. They are believed to have been assimilated during the Neolithic and early Bronze Age by the makers of the ensuing Capsian culture.

In the Tassili n'Ajjer mountains of south-eastern Algeria, cattle were herded across vast areas as early as 3000 to 2000 BCE. This reflects the origins and spread of pastoralism in the region during the Bronze Age.

Seaborne contacts between Iberia and Morocco in the first half of the third millennium BCE are thought, according to researcher Turek, to have produced the Maritime Bell Beaker pottery style. This was an early sign of Bronze Age exchange reaching north-western Africa by sea.

The Horse tradition of rock art at Tassili n'Ajjer began around 2000 BCE, when horses started appearing in its scenes. It followed the earlier cattle-herding imagery, which dates from about 3000 to 2000 BCE.

Rock art at Tassili n'Ajjer includes a distinct 'Horse' tradition, dated from around 2000 BCE. It shows that horses reached this part of the Sahara during the Bronze Age, after the earlier spread of cattle herding in the area.

The wadis running through Tassili n'Ajjer functioned as corridors linking the rocky highlands to the sandy lowlands below. These passages aided the movements of the people who occupied the highlands until as late as 1500 BCE.
